claims.text: A high-strength HEA can serve as the structural substrate.
Adding an engineered nanoscale, thermally stable lubricious surface layer to an HEA will produce stable low friction and wear across a wide temperature range.
The surface modification will preserve the HEA's robust mechanical strength.
Precipitation-strengthened HEAs are suitable candidates for high-temperature structural applications.
The proposed HEA substrate has excellent high-temperature strength and thermal stability.
The initial HEA lacks an integrated self-lubricating surface.
Controlled high-temperature oxidation or solid-lubricant deposition can create a nanoscale, thermally stable lubricious layer on an HEA.
The material will operate from cryogenic through high-temperature conditions.
Surface engineering will produce a continuous nanoscale lubricious layer.
The lubricious layer will remain chemically and structurally stable at high temperatures.
The lubricious layer will remain bonded to the underlying HEA.
The surface layer decouples tribological functionality from bulk mechanical performance.
The surface layer provides low friction and wear resistance while the HEA substrate provides strength and structural integrity.
The dual-layer material will maintain low friction and reduced wear without compromising mechanical strength across the operating range.
The dual-layer material will outperform conventional alloys that trade strength against lubrication or lubricate only over a narrow temperature range.
Traditional high-temperature alloys and untreated HEAs generally lack either broad-range self-lubrication or sufficient strength.
Layer degradation, delamination, or reaction with the substrate during thermal cycling would impair long-term performance.
Long-term layer adhesion, stability, and interfacial reactions under complex thermal and environmental cycling remain uncertain.
